articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Electricity in Product Finishing' (Digest No.52)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electricity in Product Finishing
IEE Colloquium on Electricity in Product Finishing
abstract: The author concentrates on the practical control of thyristors for producing DC on electrophoretic paint plants. The author discusses the process of electrophoretic painting and the need for pure DC and accurate control of current and voltage. The author then discusses how this can be achieved by using thyristors. Operational control using batch and continuous control is also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

abstract: The author discusses the principles of thermal spraying and the electrical systems used for producing and projecting particles. These are arc spraying, plasma spraying, and molten metal spraying. The coating process technique is described in detail and materials and applications are mentioned.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electricity in Product Finishing
abstract: The authors discuss exactly what an electroplating plant is and the types of equipment to be found there. They then go on to discuss the need for control of such a plant. Equipment options and their advantages and disadvantages are discussed. Selection of a suitable system considering work transfer, rectifier control, process temperature control, solution maintenance, process start-up, effluent treatment, and fault monitoring are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Infrared and ultra-violet systems for heating and curing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electricity in Product Finishing
abstract: Both UV and IR systems have become an accepted branch of engineering practice, not only in the UK but on a world-wide basis. Electric systems provide industry with a versatile but inexpensive energy source capable of satisfying a vast range of process requirements. When correctly applied these systems can play an important part in the drive towards energy savings, product quality, pollution abatement, higher profit margins through higher productivity, and increased competitiveness in trade on world markets. The authors discuss the applications of IR and UV in heating and curing. Equipment selection, safety and benefits are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrolytic etchant regeneration for the printed circuit board industry
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electricity in Product Finishing
abstract: In the production of printed circuit boards a very important operation is that of etching a process which results in large quantities of surplus etchant being produced, which have little or no value to the printed circuit board being produced, which have little or no value to the printed circuit board manufacturer. The Capenhurst Electrolytic Etchant Regeneration (CEER) process enables the etchant to be continuously regenerated. The only chemical losses from the system are those due to drag out, so that the purchase of replenishment chemicals is virtually eliminated. Moreover, the copper that has been etched from the boards is recovered as a pure electrolytic powder, which can be sold, and the etching operation, which was previously a costly process, can now be profitable. The author discusses both the conventional and CEER processes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Heating and metal recovery for electroplating
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electricity in Product Finishing
abstract: The author discusses the use of electricity in electroplating and anodising. He discusses how the use of immersion heaters can greatly reduce production costs and improve the consistency of the plated finish. For the cases where immersion heating is not possible the author discusses electrode boilers. Metal recovery using electrical materials recycling equipment is also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
